description: Manually reviewed research summaries, not quotations. These studies do not validate this app or establish ideal sprint angles.

sources.title: Simulations Reveal How Touchdown Kinematic Variables Affect Top Sprinting Speed: Implications for Coaching
sources.population: A three-dimensional musculoskeletal model scaled to an international-caliber adult male sprinter, simulating a symmetric top-speed step.
sources.summary: Reducing horizontal foot-to-center-of-mass touchdown distance below the model's optimum reduced speed and contact time. Changes to inter-knee touchdown distance had little effect within the tested range. Shorter touchdown distance or shorter contact was not automatically better.
sources.limitations: One model and one sprint phase do not provide an individual target. A hip landmark is not whole-body center of mass. Current angle extrema do not measure touchdown distance, braking force, or whether the foot lands too far forward.

sources.title: Determination of Foot Strike and Toe-off Event Timing during Maximal Sprint Using Kinematic Data
sources.population: Five male sprinters during acceleration, using tracked foot markers and simultaneous ground-reaction-force measurements.
sources.summary: Toe-marker vertical acceleration and position were used to locate contact events and evaluated against a force reference. This establishes a non-LLM approach under the study's measurement conditions.
sources.limitations: Tracked laboratory markers are not noisy monocular MediaPipe foot landmarks. The study does not validate this app, arbitrary camera motion, hidden shoes, or an LLM judging selected frames.

sources.title: Automatic high fidelity foot contact location and timing for elite sprinting
sources.population: Laboratory and sporting sprint recordings using a multi-camera setup.
sources.summary: The study evaluated engineered occupancy-map contact detection and fused OpenPose toe tracking for contact locations and timing. Temporal video processing can detect sprint contacts without a language model.
sources.limitations: Multi-camera results cannot be transferred to one panning phone camera. Camera calibration, event validation, and left/right tracking remain necessary for this application.

sources.title: Relationship between anthropometric and kinematic measures to practice velocity in elite American 100 m sprinters
sources.population: Nineteen male and nineteen female elite adult US sprinters; mean age about twenty-seven.
sources.summary: The reported group means for maximum upper-leg flexion differed modestly, while total thigh excursion was similar. Contact events were visually identified with high-speed video. These are descriptive results from adults.
sources.limitations: Does not test whether most high-school girls use less frontside mechanics. No individual optimal angle follows from sex, height or weight. Study angle conventions must not be treated as this app's target values.

sources.title: Kinetics and Kinematics of Sprinting in Mid and Post Peak Height Velocity Female Athletes
sources.population: Thirty-two young female athletes classified into mid- and post-peak-height-velocity groups.
sources.summary: Sprint characteristics differed across growth-related groups. The findings support considering development when discussing young athletes' sprint performance.
sources.limitations: This female-only sample does not test a girls-versus-boys frontside hypothesis. Chronological age alone does not establish maturity, and adult norms are not youth prescriptions.

sources.title: Sex differences in muscle morphology between male and female sprinters
sources.population: Adult male and female sprinters, including elite and performance-matched subgroups.
sources.summary: Muscle-volume differences depended on muscle group and the performance groups compared. Elite male and female sprinters showed similar relative muscle distribution.
sources.limitations: Body mass or sex is not a substitute for measured muscle morphology or strength. This does not prescribe an individual's sprint posture, infer a weak muscle from video or establish a high-school sex difference.

sources.title: Strength and performance asymmetry during maximal velocity sprint running
sources.population: Eight athletes with laboratory sprint and jump measurements.
sources.summary: Asymmetry patterns were individual and task-specific. Overall asymmetry was not related to sprint performance in this small sample.
sources.limitations: A video-derived contact or angle difference cannot identify a particular weak muscle. Strength capacity is one assessment question among several, requiring independent testing.

sources.title: Sprint running mechanics are associated with hamstring strain injury: a 6-month prospective cohort study of 126 elite male footballers
sources.population: Professional male football players assessed with the Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score.
sources.summary: A clinician-assessed sprint mechanics score was associated with subsequent sprint-related hamstring injuries in the studied cohort.
sources.limitations: This app does not implement or validate that score. The study cannot turn this app's angles into an injury prediction, explain a user's past injury, or establish applicability to adolescent girls.

sources.title: A comparison between common measurement systems for quantifying spatiotemporal variables during the early sprint acceleration phase
sources.population: University students sprinting with simultaneous high-speed video, optical and force-platform measurements.
sources.summary: Video and instrumented measurements showed systematic contact-time differences. Visually marked shoe contact is not interchangeable with force-defined contact.
sources.limitations: High-speed video can support reviewed event timing under controlled conditions, but this does not validate automatic foot-contact detection or the current app. Frame brackets omit other sources of error.

sources.title: Examination of 2D frontal and sagittal markerless motion capture: Implications for markerless applications
sources.population: Fifteen healthy adults walking; OpenPose compared with marker-based motion capture.
sources.summary: In sagittal recordings, occlusion substantially affected hip and knee estimates on the camera-far side. Visible-side measurements were more dependable in this setting.
sources.limitations: Walking and OpenPose results do not establish the accuracy of MediaPipe during sprinting. Visibility scores are not calibrated angle-error estimates.

sources.title: On the Importance of 'Front-Side Mechanics' in Athletics Sprinting
sources.population: Twenty-four competitive sprinters measured using high-speed three-dimensional motion capture.
sources.summary: Some front-side and back-side variables were associated with acceleration performance. The study did not find significant associations between those variables and maximum-velocity performance.
sources.limitations: Associations do not identify a universal ideal technique or show that changing an observed angle improves an individual athlete's speed. Sprint phase matters.

sources.title: 'Whip from the hip': thigh angular motion, ground contact mechanics, and running speed
sources.population: Forty participants with varied athletic backgrounds performing running trials across a range of speeds.
sources.summary: Thigh angular motion was associated with running speed across trials. The study supports examining thigh motion over a stride rather than judging a single pose in isolation.
sources.limitations: The app does not measure thigh angular velocity or ground reaction forces. An observed thigh-angle range cannot establish speed, force, or a causal performance deficit.

sources.title: VideoRun2D: Cost-Effective Markerless Motion Capture for Sprint Biomechanics
sources.population: Forty sprint recordings from five subjects; an adapted MoveNet system compared with manual annotation.
sources.summary: A specialized markerless sprint system was evaluated against manual trunk, hip and knee annotation. This illustrates the importance of checking a model against a defined reference task.
sources.limitations: The evaluated system and validation are different from this app's unmodified MediaPipe model. Its reported accuracy must not be claimed for Track Sprint AI.

sources.title: Unilateral and Bilateral Lower-Body Resistance Training Does not Transfer Equally to Sprint and Change of Direction Performance
sources.population: Thirty-three trained participants in a supervised resistance-training intervention.
sources.summary: Both squat and step-up training groups improved sprint performance, with an unclear difference between the groups for sprint outcomes.
sources.limitations: This does not show that a specific exercise will correct a video-derived joint angle. The app cannot infer a strength deficit or prescribe the study's program from footage.

sources.title: Kinematic stride cycle asymmetry is not associated with sprint performance and injury prevalence in athletic sprinters
sources.population: Competitive sprinters assessed during flying sprint trials.
sources.summary: The study did not find an association between measured stride-cycle asymmetry and sprint performance or injury prevalence in its sample.
sources.limitations: This does not prove that every asymmetry is harmless. A single oblique video cannot establish an anatomical imbalance, weakness, or injury risk.

sources.title: Angular kinematics during top speed sprinting in male intercollegiate track and field and team sport athletes
sources.population: Ninety-eight male intercollegiate athletes, including track-and-field and team-sport groups.
sources.summary: Digitized, calibrated side-on high-speed video was used to assess centrally captured stride cycles. Angular positions associated with speed in the combined sample often did not within sport groups; similarly fast groups used different positions. Angular motion rates were associated with speed within groups.
sources.limitations: Associations do not establish a personal correction or ideal angle. The protocol used verified timing, selected events and manual digitization; it does not validate panning MediaPipe trajectories or infer muscle power from an angle.

sources.title: Does restricting arm motion compromise short sprint running performance?
sources.population: Seventeen track-and-field and team-sport athletes performing normal and folded-arm thirty-metre sprints.
sources.summary: The experiment compared sprint performance under normal arm motion and deliberately restricted arm motion after habituation. It studied a large imposed change in arm use rather than small natural left-right angle differences.
sources.limitations: The experiment does not provide an ideal elbow angle, diagnose a weak side, quantify this athlete's arm power or establish that correcting a small observed asymmetry improves performance. Current arm measurements are projected estimates and need visibility checks.
